h: Shale, Bings and the Story of a New Town
p: Ever wondered about those strange flat-topped, reddish hills you pass on the motorway through West Lothian? They're bings, giant heaps of waste from the shale oil industry, and they're a big part of the story you'll pick up at Almond Valley. The industry was kick-started in the 1850s by a Scottish chemist called James Young, nicknamed Paraffin Young, who worked out how to get oil from shale. For decades it shaped the villages and landscape round here, and some of the bings, like the Five Sisters near West Calder, are now protected landmarks in their own right.

That gives older children a proper hook. Ask them to spot the bings on the way home, and suddenly a day of tractors and goats has a real-world twist. Little ones won't care a jot about oil, of course, so let them lead in the farmyard and play areas, and save the history for when they need a sit-down. A change of clothes is handy, as farm play and puddles go hand in hand.

Livingston itself is a new town, designated in 1962, which is why the town centre feels so modern compared with the old villages around it. For a breather afterwards, Almondell and Calderwood Country Park follows the River Almond with woodland walks and a visitor centre. Linlithgow, with its roofless royal palace by the loch where Mary Queen of Scots was born, is a short drive north and makes a fabulous second stop. Between the shale, the palace and the farm animals, it's a surprisingly rich slice of Scotland for one weekend.
